stem.en: How did Lewis Carroll feel about interviews?

options.en: He had a horror of them and never consented to be interviewed

explanation.en: Carroll had a horror of interviewers and never agreed to be interviewed.

stem.en: Which writer compared interviews to thumbprints on his windpipe?

explanation.en: Saul Bellow used the image of thumbprints on his windpipe.

stem.en: According to Denis Brian, what is one benefit of interviews?

options.en: More of us know more about our contemporaries

explanation.en: Brian argued that, thanks to interviews, people know more about their contemporaries.

stem.en: Why do some people see the interview as an intrusion?

options.en: It pries into their private lives
It is printed in small type

explanation.en: Critics feel interviews intrude into private life without justification.

stem.en: Silvester compares the feeling of being diminished by interviews to the belief that

options.en: speech is silver and silence is gold
a photograph can steal a person's soul

explanation.en: He mentions the belief in some cultures that photographing a person steals their soul.

stem.en: What does Silvester suggest about the position of the interviewer today?

options.en: The interviewer holds great power and influence
The interviewer must always be a celebrity

explanation.en: He notes that the interviewer now has a position of great power and influence.

stem.en: What does Eco mean by "interstices"?

options.en: Small empty spaces or gaps in time

explanation.en: Interstices are small gaps, such as time spent waiting, which Eco uses to work.

stem.en: How does Eco describe himself?

options.en: As a university professor who writes novels on Sundays

explanation.en: He sees himself mainly as an academic who writes novels in his spare time.

stem.en: Semiotics, one of Eco's fields, is the study of

explanation.en: Semiotics is the study of signs and how meaning is made.

stem.en: What is special about Eco's scholarly writing?

options.en: It is written only in Latin
It has a narrative quality, telling the story of his research

explanation.en: Eco says he narrates the story of his research, including trials and errors.

stem.en: The Name of the Rose is described as

options.en: a detective story that also explores metaphysics, theology and medieval history

explanation.en: It works on the surface as a detective novel but deals with serious ideas.

stem.en: Which reason does Eco give for the success of The Name of the Rose?

options.en: It was very short and easy to read
It was made compulsory in schools
Timing: it might not have succeeded if written ten years earlier or later

explanation.en: He calls the success a mystery and suggests timing played a part.

stem.en: What view about readers does Eco challenge?

options.en: That readers want only easy, light books

explanation.en: The success of a serious novel shows that readers can enjoy challenging books.

stem.en: The cricketer's complaint about a private remark being printed reflects which criticism of interviews in Part I?

options.en: That interviews are a supreme source of truth
That interviews help us know our contemporaries
That interviews can be an intrusion into private life
That interviews are a recent invention

explanation.en: Printing an off-the-record remark is the kind of intrusion critics of the interview complain about.

passage.en: A popular cricketer gave forty interviews during a single tour. In a podcast later, he said that most journalists asked the same three questions and that one reporter had printed a private remark he had made off the record. Still, he admitted that a long, thoughtful interview with a sports magazine had helped fans understand his struggle with injury. He now gives fewer interviews and chooses interviewers who prepare carefully.

stem.en: The cricketer's praise of the long magazine interview supports whose view?

options.en: Denis Brian's, that interviews help us know our contemporaries
Lewis Carroll's, that interviews should be refused

explanation.en: The thoughtful interview helped fans understand him, supporting the positive view of interviews.
